headline: Hidden cameras, glove-trained robots and a flickering headset: what to trust?
teaser: Can an exam stay fair when AI fits in a button? Who should profit when workers teach robots? When is a promising result really proof?

articles.title: Can an Exam Stay Fair When AI Fits in a Button?
articles.dek: Before the Suneung, South Korea is inspecting students' glasses and shirt buttons for AI cheating devices. Can tighter security protect fairness, or does the scandal show that exams themselves must change?

sources.name: The Telegraph via Yahoo News, Nov 16, 2026

paras: On Thursday, more than half a million South Korean students will sit the Suneung, the national college entrance exam that can shape their university choices, careers and, many believe, the rest of their lives. The exam is so important that flights are rescheduled during the listening test and police help late students reach their test centres. This year, however, the most talked-about preparation is not happening in classrooms. It is happening at the doors of exam rooms, where staff will examine students' glasses, watches, collars and even shirt buttons, looking for hidden cameras linked to AI.

The sudden alarm was triggered by a scandal in a different test. Han Won-seok, a 34-year-old who had come first in this year's national exam for tax accountants, admitted in a YouTube video that his score was not entirely his own. In both rounds of the exam, he said, he used a miniature camera to photograph the questions, sent the images to a generative AI system, and read the answers on a small screen. In the first round he answered 159 of 160 multiple-choice questions correctly. He apologised and was questioned by police on Tuesday. His confession raised an uncomfortable question: if one person could defeat a professional exam so easily, how many others had tried, and had anyone done it in the Suneung?

Online, some claimed that the answer was yes. An anonymous user on a popular Korean forum wrote that they had cheated on the 2024 Suneung with a camera disguised as a shirt button and later entered medical school. The claim could not be verified, and it may be false, but it spread quickly. A YouTuber with more than two million subscribers even urged the Education Ministry to postpone the exam, noting that it had been delayed before, after a 2017 earthquake and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The government chose not to delay. Instead, at a Cabinet meeting two days before the exam, it announced a package of emergency measures. All smartphones and other smart devices will be switched off and collected, and simply possessing one during the test can be treated as cheating. Bags must stay outside exam rooms, and each of the country's 1,312 test centres will have staff assigned to spot smart glasses. The science ministry has been asked to study switching off public Wi-Fi at test sites, and officials are considering metal and radio-frequency detectors for future exams. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook described AI-assisted cheating as a "social evil", and lawmakers have proposed extending the exam ban for cheaters from one year to ten.

Supporters argue that strict rules are the only reasonable response. The Suneung matters precisely because it is seen as fair: every student answers the same questions under the same conditions, regardless of family wealth or connections. As one Hanyang University professor put it, if AI devices can compromise this exam, "the issue goes far beyond a single act of cheating." From this perspective, inspecting glasses is a small inconvenience compared with the damage that a single proven case could do to public trust.

Critics, however, doubt that the measures will work. A teachers' union official said he did not think the plan was "really an effective response", and an education commentator warned that staff cannot reliably spot new smart glasses just by looking. Even Deputy Education Minister Choi Eun-ok acknowledged that it is "not easy to detect 100 per cent of cheating without completely blocking communications." Each new rule, critics say, simply encourages cheaters to find smaller and better-hidden devices, creating an arms race that schools are unlikely to win.

A third group of educators believes the scandal points to a deeper problem. If an AI system can answer a test almost perfectly within seconds, they argue, the test may be measuring the kind of knowledge that machines already handle well, such as recalling facts and applying familiar procedures. Some suggest giving more weight to tasks that are harder to outsource, such as supervised essays, oral examinations or projects completed over time. Others reply that such assessments are expensive, harder to score consistently and more open to the advantages of wealthy families, which is exactly what a standardized exam was designed to prevent.

For now, the goal is simply to get through Thursday without a scandal, but the debate will not end when the exam does. Many countries, including China with its gaokao, rely on high-stakes exams to distribute limited university places in a way the public accepts as fair. South Korea's experience suggests that protecting that fairness may require more than better detectors; it may also require rethinking what an exam is meant to measure in an age when any student could, in theory, carry a genius in a button.

speak.p: Some people think a single national exam is the fairest way to decide university admission. Others think universities should also use essays, interviews and long-term projects. Which approach do you prefer, and why?
speak.hint: State your view → reason 1 (fairness / equal conditions) + example → reason 2 (what the method really measures) + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: This week South Korea introduced strict security measures, including checking students' glasses and shirt buttons, to stop AI-assisted cheating in its national college entrance exam. Some people say these measures are necessary to protect fairness; others say they treat every student as a suspect and will not stop determined cheaters. In your opinion, what is the best way for schools to deal with the risk of AI cheating in important exams? (Mina says: Strict security is the only realistic answer. A national exam is fair only if everyone follows the same rules, so checking devices and punishing cheaters severely protects honest students. A few minutes of inspection is a small price to pay.) (Daniel says: I think security alone will fail, because the devices keep getting smaller. Schools should change the exams themselves, for example by adding supervised essays or oral tests that an AI hidden in a button cannot easily answer.)
steps: Decide your position: stricter security, new types of exams, or a mix.
Give one main reason, such as fairness or the limits of detection.
Respond to Mina or Daniel: agree with one point and challenge another.
Finish with a clear one-sentence conclusion.

articles.title: Workers in Sensor Gloves Are Teaching Robots to Use Their Hands
articles.dek: A robotics start-up has raised $500 million to give machines human-like hands, using data recorded from workers' gloves. Is this the breakthrough robots need, and who benefits from the skills it captures?

sources.name: Genesis AI press release (PR Newswire), Nov 17, 2026

paras: Ask a computer to play chess and it will probably beat you. Ask a robot to fold a T-shirt, peel a sticker off a roll or tie a knot, and it will probably fail. Scientists call this puzzle Moravec's paradox: tasks that feel difficult to humans, such as calculation, are often easy for computers, while tasks that feel effortless, such as using our hands, are extremely hard for them. This week, a young American company called Genesis AI announced that investors had given it $500 million to solve this problem, valuing the company at $3.5 billion. Its strategy depends on an unusual source of knowledge: ordinary workers wearing special gloves.

The reason dexterity is so difficult for machines is partly mechanical and partly a matter of data. A human hand combines dozens of joints with thousands of touch sensors, constantly adjusting its grip without conscious thought. AI chatbots became powerful by learning from enormous amounts of text on the internet, but there is no comparable library of touch. Almost nobody has recorded, in precise numbers, how hard a person presses when lifting an egg or how their fingers move when threading a cable. As Genesis puts it, most human physical skills have simply never been written down.

To fill that gap, the company has given sensor-equipped gloves and head-mounted cameras to more than 100 workers around the world. As they do their normal jobs, the gloves record the movement of each finger and the force it applies, while the cameras capture what the workers see. The robots then wear the same kind of glove, and their mechanical hands are built to match human proportions, so that a movement recorded on a person can be transferred directly to a machine. Genesis also uses computer simulation, based on a physics method co-developed by one of its advisers, to generate millions of additional practice examples.

In a demonstration for journalists, robotic arms running the company's software packed items into a box, sealed it with tape and attached a label. On a second attempt, however, a robot dropped a box and struggled to peel a small label from its backing. Rather than hiding these errors, the company described them as "hiccup data", mistakes that can be fed back into the model so it learns to recover. Its chief executive, Zhou Xian, believes that the quality of data matters far more than clever design: he estimates that the model's architecture contributes "maybe 10%" of the final result. "We have all the recipes," he said. "It's just about execution."

Supporters see enormous potential. Many countries face shortages of workers for repetitive, tiring or dangerous jobs, from sorting parcels in warehouses to handling samples in laboratories. Genesis plans to start with factories, logistics and labs, and later move into hotels, healthcare and eventually homes. Its main robot, called Eno, has a wheeled base and two arms, and each of its hands can move in 20 independent, motor-driven ways. Investors including the chipmakers Nvidia and AMD clearly believe that whoever teaches robots to use their hands will unlock a huge market.

Skeptics urge caution. Robotics has what one technology writer calls a "demo problem": impressive videos can be sped up, carefully selected or secretly controlled by a human operator. The company itself admits that its robotic hands currently last only a few weeks of regular work before they need replacing, and it has built only 30 to 40 Eno robots so far. One rival founder claimed that there are "literally zero robot hands deployed right now doing routine work." Until robots perform reliably for months in real workplaces, he and others argue, the technology remains a promise rather than a product.

There is also an ethical question that the funding announcement did not address. The workers wearing the gloves are, in effect, teaching machines to do jobs like their own. Reports on the deal did not explain how these workers are paid for their data or what control they have over recordings of their movements. Some economists argue that such technology will free people from exhausting physical labour and create new kinds of work; others worry that the benefits will flow mainly to companies and investors, while the people whose skills made the robots possible receive little in return.

The story of Genesis therefore raises a question that reaches beyond one company. As AI moves from screens into the physical world, human skill itself becomes valuable training material. Whether that leads to safer, easier work for everyone or simply to cheaper machines may depend less on how clever the robots become and more on the rules societies set for who owns, and profits from, the knowledge in our hands.

articles.title: Did the "Light and Sound" Alzheimer's Headset Fail? It Depends How You Read the Data
articles.dek: A year-long trial of a flickering headset for Alzheimer's missed its main goal, yet one group of patients seemed to benefit. How should we judge a result that is both disappointing and promising?
paras: For nearly a decade, an unusual idea has attracted both excitement and doubt in Alzheimer's research: that flickering lights and buzzing sounds might slow the disease. This week, the idea faced its biggest test so far. Cognito Therapeutics, a company based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, presented the results of a year-long trial of its headset, called Spectris, at a major Alzheimer's conference in Boston. Within hours, the news coverage split in two. One leading science journal reported that the therapy had "flopped"; a local newspaper said it "may slow Alzheimer's symptoms in some patients." Both headlines were, in a sense, accurate, and understanding why reveals a great deal about how medical evidence works.

The science behind the device begins with brain rhythms. Groups of neurons fire together in regular waves, and one fast pattern, known as gamma oscillations, at around 40 cycles per second, is linked to attention and memory. In Alzheimer's disease, these rhythms weaken early. In 2016, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology reported that exposing mice to light flickering 40 times a second reduced the sticky amyloid plaques associated with the disease. Two of the scientists involved went on to found Cognito, and the company built a device that looks like a pair of glasses attached to headphones and is used at home for about an hour a day.

The new trial, called HOPE, was designed to answer a clear question. It enrolled 673 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's and randomly assigned them to use either the real device or a "sham" version that looked similar but did not deliver the 40-hertz stimulation. Neither the patients nor the researchers knew who received which, a design known as double-blind. Before the trial began, the company chose a single primary endpoint, a combined score of thinking and everyday abilities, to decide whether the device worked.

On that main measure, the device failed. Across all participants, there was no meaningful difference between the real and the sham groups. The company's chief executive, Christian Howell, admitted that the team had hoped to see an effect in the full population and did not. However, when the researchers looked only at the 395 people with mild disease, the picture changed. In this group, daily functioning declined 56% more slowly than in the sham group, and a standard clinical rating declined 47% more slowly. Patients who used the device on at least 70% of days appeared to benefit even more, while those with more advanced disease showed little improvement.

For the company, these numbers are a reason for optimism. Howell argues that medical devices should be judged on whether their benefits outweigh their risks, not on a single statistical target, and the headset appears to be relatively safe: its most common side effects were headaches and ringing in the ears. By comparison, the antibody drugs recently approved for Alzheimer's slow decline by roughly 20 to 30% but can cause swelling or bleeding in the brain. Cognito plans to ask the US Food and Drug Administration for authorization to treat mild Alzheimer's, with a filing expected in 2027.

Many independent experts, however, remain unconvinced. Paul Aisen of the University of Southern California called the overall result "simply negative" and described the subgroup findings as exploratory. The problem is statistical: when researchers divide a trial into many smaller groups after seeing the data, some groups will show impressive results purely by chance. Daniel Gillen of the University of California, Irvine, made a related point about adherence. People who faithfully use a treatment every day may differ from those who do not, for example by being healthier or having more family support, so their better outcomes do not prove that the device caused the improvement. The results have also not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

There are practical questions, too. Fewer than half of the patients with mild disease used the device on at least 70% of days, and a researcher at Mount Sinai doubted that an hour of daily flickering is realistic for many older people. Meanwhile, several companies already sell unproven 40-hertz products directly to consumers, and experts worry that mixed headlines could encourage desperate families to spend money on devices with no reliable evidence behind them.

The HOPE trial will not settle the debate. What it offers instead is a lesson in reading scientific news. A trial's pre-planned main result carries the most weight; a promising subgroup is a clue that deserves a new, carefully designed study, not a conclusion. For the millions of families affected by Alzheimer's, hope is understandable, and the device may yet prove useful for some patients. But as this case shows, the gap between "it might work for some people" and "it works" is exactly where good science has to do its most careful thinking.
